name: Battery size
seoTitle: Battery size Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Battery size: work out application load from the voltage and the remaining charge. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Battery size calculator the voltage, the remaining charge, the load current and the remaining capacity and it returns application load. Think of it as a shortcut for whatever you happen to be working on. The results leave the screen the moment you edit a field; press Calculate and they come back updated, so a single changed input shows its own effect.

sections.title: How does the Battery size calculator work?
sections.html:
The Battery size calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports application load in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the battery type); then you type in the voltage, the remaining charge, the load current and the remaining capacity.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as lead-acid and lithium-ion. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in %.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in amperes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in ampere hours. The unit chip switches it to any of the 9 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Battery size calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Application load=load current × voltage
Required duration=(1 ÷ 100) × remaining capacity × (100 − remaining charge) ÷ load current
Remaining capacity=-5000 × load current × required duration ÷ (remaining charge × required duration + 30 × remaining charge − 100 × required duration − 3000)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Battery type set to Lead-acid, Voltage = 10 V and Load current = 10 A. The calculator returns Application load = 100 W.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Application load = 100 W should be roughly the size you expected from Battery type set to Lead-acid and Voltage = 10 V.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in watts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.
  • Shown in hours, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Shown in ampere hours, and convertible to any of the 9 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Power, opening in watts
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Time, opening in hours
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Electric charge, opening in ampere hours
  • Electric charge, opening in ampere hours

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Battery size calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the voltage, the remaining charge and the load current — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Battery size calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns application load, derived from the voltage, the remaining charge and the load current. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Battery size calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the voltage, the remaining charge, the load current and the remaining capacity, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter application load in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Application load opens in watts and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Application load = 100 W. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Battery size calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
